chapters.title: Build an intuition
chapters.text: Let us understand load balancing. A school has three lunch counters. A helper sends each child to an open counter instead of letting everyone crowd around the first. If a counter closes, the helper stops using it. But if all counters share one empty kitchen, the helper cannot create food. Likewise, distributing requests does not remove a shared database bottleneck. One address receives requests and shares them across healthy copies of your application. It chooses a destination; it does not create extra servers or make slow database queries disappear.

chapters.title: Follow the normal path
chapters.text: Follow the normal path. Visitors send event requests to one endpoint. The load balancer selects an application target so visitors do not need to know individual server addresses. Alternate requests between App A and App B. This shares turns, but a slow request can still occupy one target much longer than another. In our fictional SeatSpot ticket app, many people open the same event at once. One application instance becomes overloaded while a second has spare capacity. A load balancer makes the spare capacity reachable through the same public endpoint.

chapters.title: Predict a failure
chapters.text: Now change one condition. App A stops passing readiness checks. Detection takes time; requests already in flight may fail and must be handled safely by the client. A common misunderstanding is this: Round robin means equal CPU usage. It shares turns; request cost and connection lifetime can differ. Think about this. App A fails. Can App B always take all its traffic? Pause the video and make your prediction. Only if App B and the shared dependencies have enough tested spare capacity. Health checks also take time to remove App A.

chapters.title: Work through an example
chapters.text: Let us reason with a concrete example. Suppose one tested replica handles 200 requests/second within the latency objective and the expected peak is 450. Three replicas provide 600 requests/second in the simplified model. Losing one leaves 400, below the peak. Four leave 600 after one failure. Real capacity must be load-tested with the database and dependencies. Use four if that failure headroom is required and affordable. Monitor per-target latency, error rate and queueing; do not infer usable capacity from instance count alone. These figures are teaching examples, not production guarantees.

chapters.title: Choose and apply
chapters.text: Turn the idea into a design decision. New requests go to App B after the target is removed. App B needs enough spare capacity; routing cannot manufacture capacity during an outage. Both copies use the same order system. A repeated booking request carries the same idempotency key so a lost response does not charge twice. When you try the practice task, look for this result. The surviving target receives new traffic, but the database remains shared.

chapters.title: Explain it back
chapters.text: Check your understanding. Check latency and errors at the balancer, application and database. If both applications wait on the database, adding routing rules will not fix that bottleneck. Here is a challenge. You have three replicas each safe at 150 requests/second. Peak demand is 350. Can you survive one replica failing? Pause before the answer. After a failure, two replicas provide 300, below 350. Four total leave 450 after one failure in this simplified model. Also test dependency limits and the actual request mix. For an interview, defend a routing policy, session state and failure headroom. Say what you would measure, not only which tool you would buy.

chapters.title: Build an intuition
chapters.text: Let us understand auto scaling. A shop manager sees a long checkout queue and opens another counter. Opening takes time: someone must arrive, sign in and prepare the till. Closing every quiet counter immediately would cause a new queue a minute later. The manager needs minimum staffing and patience, not just a rule that reacts to every small change. Auto scaling changes capacity automatically when measured demand changes. A controller observes a signal, chooses a replica count and waits for new capacity to become ready. It is a delayed feedback loop, not instant unlimited capacity.

chapters.title: Follow the normal path
chapters.text: Follow the normal path. The application serves visitors while metrics record utilization and request behavior. Select a signal related to the constrained resource, not simply the easiest chart. The controller compares the observed signal with a configured target and computes a desired replica count within minimum and maximum limits. SeatSpot traffic grows before a popular sale. Manual scaling may arrive too late, while leaving peak capacity running all day wastes resources. Automatic control can help, provided start-up delay and dependency limits are included.

chapters.title: Predict a failure
chapters.text: Now change one condition. The controller requests more replicas. Scheduling, image download, initialization and health checks take time. Desired capacity and ready capacity can differ. A common misunderstanding is this: Automatic scaling is instant. Observation, scheduling, image startup and readiness all take time. Think about this. CPU is low while requests wait on a database. Should CPU scaling be your only signal? Pause the video and make your prediction. No. CPU can be low during I/O waits. Inspect latency, concurrency, database waits and the actual constrained resource.

chapters.title: Work through an example
chapters.text: Let us reason with a concrete example. Four replicas average 80% CPU. The target is 50%, assuming similar replicas and CPU-bound work. A simplified estimate is ceil(4 × 80 / 50) = 7 replicas. This is a teaching estimate; real controllers apply tolerances, readiness handling and other policies. Check whether seven replicas can start, whether their total database connections fit, and whether latency improves. A replica recommendation is not proof the system is safe. These figures are teaching examples, not production guarantees.

chapters.title: Choose and apply
chapters.text: Turn the idea into a design decision. Only ready replicas should receive normal traffic. If nodes or quotas are exhausted, a controller cannot create the missing physical capacity by itself. More application copies can increase database connections. Limit aggregate concurrency so solving an application bottleneck does not create a database outage. When you try the practice task, look for this result. Seven is a simplified recommendation, not seven instantly ready or safe servers.

chapters.title: Explain it back
chapters.text: Check your understanding. After demand falls, stabilization prevents rapid shrinking and regrowth. Drain work before removing replicas and keep enough minimum capacity for the next burst. Here is a challenge. A queue receives 120 jobs/second. Each worker handles 20. How many workers stop backlog growth, and why might you need more? Pause before the answer. Six workers match the average under ideal assumptions. More are needed to drain existing backlog and tolerate failures or variable duration, within downstream safety limits. Monitor oldest-job age, not just queue size. For an interview, choose metrics, minimums, maximums and stabilization. Say what you would measure, not only which tool you would buy.

chapters.title: Build an intuition
chapters.text: Let us understand high availability. A school keeps two water pumps so one can help when the other stops. If both use the same broken power line, two pumps do not solve the problem. Availability depends on the whole chain and on how quickly people notice and recover, not just the number of pumps. High availability means meeting an agreed target for successful service over time. Redundant components and recovery reduce downtime, but a system can never promise that nothing will ever fail.

chapters.title: Follow the normal path
chapters.text: Follow the normal path. For this example, success means a correct booking response within its latency objective. A homepage response alone does not measure the same user outcome. Applications run in separate zones behind a resilient entry point. The goal is to avoid losing every application copy to the same local failure. SeatSpot must keep ticket browsing and booking usable when a machine or zone fails. Different features can have different objectives: cached event descriptions may remain available even if booking is temporarily paused to protect correct seat allocation.

chapters.title: Predict a failure
chapters.text: Now change one condition. Zone A becomes unavailable. Detection and rerouting consume time, and requests already in flight may fail. The objective allows an explicitly measured error budget. A common misunderstanding is this: Two replicas guarantee availability. Shared power, data, credentials or control planes can fail both replicas. Think about this. Two apps run on different machines but use one unprotected database. Is the complete booking path redundant? Pause the video and make your prediction. No. A database failure can still stop both apps. Follow the entire user operation, not only the web tier.

chapters.title: Work through an example
chapters.text: Let us reason with a concrete example. An agreed objective is 99.9% time availability over an illustrative 30-day month. 30 × 24 × 60 = 43,200 minutes. A 0.1% unavailability budget is 43.2 minutes. Request-based indicators use failed eligible requests instead, so do not mix the two measurements. Choose the objective from business needs and recovery cost. Measure actual booking success separately from whether the homepage responds. These figures are teaching examples, not production guarantees.

chapters.title: Choose and apply
chapters.text: Turn the idea into a design decision. Zone B receives new work. It must have enough capacity, network access and working credentials to serve the actual user operation. Both application copies need a suitable data service. A single unprotected database can still interrupt bookings even when both application zones are healthy. When you try the practice task, look for this result. The illustrative time budget is 43.2 minutes; a request-based SLI uses different units.

chapters.title: Explain it back
chapters.text: Check your understanding. Run a controlled failure and measure booking success and recovery time. Availability is demonstrated by user outcomes, not by counting boxes in a diagram. Here is a challenge. Two application replicas run in one zone. A second zone is added. List three things to verify before calling the service highly available. Pause before the answer. Check traffic failover/detection, data-layer availability and consistency, and survivor capacity. Also test shared authentication, DNS and configuration dependencies using the agreed user-visible indicator. For an interview, define the SLI, time window, failover and survivor capacity. Say what you would measure, not only which tool you would buy.

chapters.title: Build an intuition
chapters.text: Let us understand fault tolerance. A bicycle with a spare light can still be seen when the main light breaks. But that spare light cannot fix a broken frame. A useful plan names the fault and the remaining safe behavior. A website might keep showing events when its recommendation feature fails while refusing to sell a seat it cannot confirm. Fault tolerance is the ability to keep required behavior correct when specified components fail. Name the failure you tolerate and the degraded behavior you allow. It is not a claim of immunity to every possible fault.

chapters.title: Follow the normal path
chapters.text: Follow the normal path. The event page needs correct booking information, but recommendations are optional. Give these paths different deadlines and resource budgets. Recommendations stop responding. Without a boundary, waiting calls can consume all connections or workers and affect otherwise healthy operations. A slow optional recommendation service should not use every request thread and prevent checkout. SeatSpot isolates optional work and keeps a safe core path instead of treating every dependency as equally critical.

chapters.title: Predict a failure
chapters.text: Now change one condition. The timeout guard ends waiting for optional work. This protects local resources but does not prove a remote write was cancelled or never happened. A common misunderstanding is this: A timeout means the remote action did not happen. A timeout describes your observation, not the remote side effect. Think about this. A payment call times out. Is it safe to retry with a fresh order ID? Pause the video and make your prediction. No. The first charge may have succeeded. Reuse a stable idempotency identity and reconcile the unknown outcome.

chapters.title: Work through an example
chapters.text: Let us reason with a concrete example. A page fans out to three optional services with an overall 800 ms deadline. One dependency stalls for ten seconds. A 200 ms dependency timeout can preserve some page budget, but sequential calls, retries and rendering time must also fit inside 800 ms. Timeouts are not independent free budgets. Return the essential event page without recommendations; keep seat reservations and payment outcomes authoritative. Isolate resource pools so optional failures cannot consume core capacity. These figures are teaching examples, not production guarantees.

chapters.title: Choose and apply
chapters.text: Turn the idea into a design decision. Render the essential page without suggestions. Do not turn an uncertain payment outcome into a success message just to make the page appear healthy. If a retry is appropriate, limit attempts and use backoff with jitter. Preserve one operation identity for side effects so retries do not create duplicate business actions. When you try the practice task, look for this result. Recommendations can be omitted; a confirmed payment must not be invented.

chapters.title: Explain it back
chapters.text: Check your understanding. Inject a slow response and a lost reply in a safe test environment. Verify core capacity and user-visible correctness rather than only testing a clean server shutdown. Here is a challenge. The payment provider times out after you send a charge. What should the booking UI say and what should the backend do? Pause before the answer. Show a pending/unknown outcome rather than success or automatic failure. Reconcile by the same idempotency key/provider reference and update the order state. Avoid issuing a new independent charge. For an interview, bound retries, cancellation and concurrency independently. Say what you would measure, not only which tool you would buy.

chapters.title: Build an intuition
chapters.text: Let us understand horizontal scaling. A teacher asks three helpers to check homework instead of giving one helper a faster pen. This helps if papers can be divided. It does not help much if every paper must wait for one locked answer book. Shared resources and coordination decide whether more helpers actually increase throughput. Horizontal scaling adds more machines or application copies. Work must be shareable between them. It differs from auto scaling: horizontal describes the direction of growth; automatic describes how the decision is made.

chapters.title: Follow the normal path
chapters.text: Follow the normal path. One application serves event pages. Its safe measured capacity is finite, and a restart can interrupt every request reaching that copy. Deploy the same application on another machine or process. Horizontal scaling adds peers rather than increasing resources inside the original machine. SeatSpot can run several stateless event-page replicas during a sale. A user may reach a different copy on the next request, so login state, uploaded files and reservations cannot silently live only in one replica memory.

chapters.title: Predict a failure
chapters.text: Now change one condition. Routing sends requests to ready replicas. Balance according to workload characteristics; more boxes are useful only when requests can reach them. A common misunderstanding is this: More app copies automatically scale database writes. The write owner, locks and connection limits can still constrain throughput. Think about this. Four copies reach 250 requests/second when one reaches 100. Did capacity grow four times? Pause the video and make your prediction. No. The measured efficiency is 62.5% of the ideal 400. Investigate the shared bottleneck before adding more replicas.

chapters.title: Work through an example
chapters.text: Let us reason with a concrete example. One replica safely serves 100 requests/second. A load test with four replicas reaches only 250. Ideal linear scaling would suggest 400, but the measured efficiency is 250/400 = 62.5%. This number describes the experiment, not a universal law. Investigate database locking, shared CPU, connection limits and the serial part before adding another four replicas. Re-test after each change. These figures are teaching examples, not production guarantees.

chapters.title: Choose and apply
chapters.text: Turn the idea into a design decision. Both replicas use the same appropriate storage for files, sessions or records. A file written only to Replica A will not magically appear on Replica B. If every request waits on one locked database operation, extra applications may add waiting instead of throughput. Trace and load-test the complete path. When you try the practice task, look for this result. A gap from ideal scaling is a diagnostic clue, not proof which dependency is slow.

chapters.title: Explain it back
chapters.text: Check your understanding. Compare throughput and tail latency before and after scaling. Also remove one replica to check that remaining copies serve users correctly with available capacity. Here is a challenge. An upload is saved to App A local disk. The next download request reaches App B. Propose a fix. Pause before the answer. Store the file in a shared durable object store and keep metadata/access rules in an authoritative store. Stream or redirect authorized downloads from that shared location. Do not depend on sticky sessions for durability. For an interview, discuss state, job ownership, database limits and real load tests. Say what you would measure, not only which tool you would buy.

horizontal-scaling.narration: Kokoro v1.0 · af_heart · pre-generated English female voice

chapters.title: Build an intuition
chapters.text: Let us understand vertical scaling. A student replaces a tiny desk with a larger desk. More books fit, but there is still one desk. A bigger desk does not solve every problem: a lost key to the room still blocks access. Likewise, extra memory helps a memory bottleneck but may not help a slow external payment call. Vertical scaling gives one machine more CPU, memory, storage or throughput. It can be the simplest improvement, but it has a size ceiling and does not create a second copy for failover.

chapters.title: Follow the normal path
chapters.text: Follow the normal path. The application is slow. Inspect whether requests wait on CPU, memory, storage, locks or another service before selecting a bigger machine. Give the same database more appropriate resources. This is vertical scaling because the number of independent database copies has not increased. A SeatSpot database may benefit from more memory for its working set before the team considers sharding. First measure the constraint rather than buying a larger machine because the site feels slow.

chapters.title: Predict a failure
chapters.text: Now change one condition. More memory can hold more of the hot working set. If disk reads were the bottleneck, the experiment may show lower latency. A common misunderstanding is this: A larger instance is a second failover copy. It remains one instance unless a separate redundancy design exists. Think about this. A payment provider takes five seconds. Will doubling your app RAM necessarily fix it? Pause the video and make your prediction. No. Extra RAM does not shorten an external provider delay. Measure the critical path first.

chapters.title: Work through an example
chapters.text: Let us reason with a concrete example. The database reads a 12 GB hot dataset but has only 4 GB available for useful caching. A larger memory budget may improve hit rate; the actual benefit depends on access patterns, other memory users and query plans. Doubling RAM is not a promise of double throughput. Profile the working set and expensive queries, test a larger instance in a safe environment and measure tail latency and restart behavior. These figures are teaching examples, not production guarantees.

chapters.title: Choose and apply
chapters.text: Turn the idea into a design decision. A size change may restart or fail over the database. Use the actual platform procedure and verify what users see during the transition. Repeat the same controlled workload. Compare throughput, tail latency, waits and cost; do not use machine size as the success metric. When you try the practice task, look for this result. A resize is justified by observed improvement and operational constraints, not instance size alone.

chapters.title: Explain it back
chapters.text: Check your understanding. The larger machine still needs redundancy and backups. If the machine fails or reaches its size ceiling, a different design decision is needed. Here is a challenge. CPU is idle but one SQL query waits on a lock. Will twice as many cores fix it? Pause before the answer. Probably not. Inspect the blocking transaction, query and locking strategy. Extra cores do not release the lock. Re-test after addressing the measured contention. For an interview, choose a resource using profiling and compare cost. Say what you would measure, not only which tool you would buy.

chapters.title: Build an intuition
chapters.text: Let us understand caching. You keep a timetable on your desk instead of walking to the office every time. It is fast, but a changed timetable makes your copy wrong. The expiry time tells you when to check again; it does not make the copy correct until then. A cache keeps a reusable copy so future reads can avoid slower work. Copies can become stale or disappear. Decide what may be cached, for how long and who is allowed to read it.

chapters.title: Follow the normal path
chapters.text: Follow the normal path. The reader asks for a public event description. The key identifies the resource and representation; private results need appropriate identity scoping. A reusable cached value returns quickly. Its age matters: a fast response can still be too stale for the business operation. SeatSpot event descriptions change rarely and are read often. They are good cache candidates. Available-seat ownership and payment outcomes need stricter correctness rules than a public description.

chapters.title: Predict a failure
chapters.text: Now change one condition. If the value is absent or expired, fetch from the source of truth. A miss is normal and must have bounded latency and safe error handling. A common misunderstanding is this: A cache copy is always current until TTL expires. It can become stale immediately after a source update; expiry is not a correctness guarantee. Think about this. A popular key expires for every visitor at once. What load reaches the database? Pause the video and make your prediction. Many concurrent misses can refill the same value. Coalesce work, stagger expiry or serve controlled stale data where allowed.

chapters.title: Work through an example
chapters.text: Let us reason with a concrete example. An illustrative endpoint receives 1,000 reads/second with an 80% cache hit rate. About 200 reads/second reach the source in the simplified model. After a cache outage, the source may suddenly receive all 1,000. Test the cold-cache path, bound concurrent refill work and specify acceptable staleness for descriptions. Do not use the estimate to promise production capacity. These figures are teaching examples, not production guarantees.

chapters.title: Choose and apply
chapters.text: Turn the idea into a design decision. Many readers may miss the same hot key together. Coalesce loads or bound refill work so the cache does not amplify pressure on the database. Populate the cache with an explicit lifetime. Plan what happens after an update and whether serving an older value is acceptable during refresh. When you try the practice task, look for this result. At 1,000 reads/second, source demand can jump from about 200 to 1,000 when the cache disappears.

chapters.title: Explain it back
chapters.text: Check your understanding. Remove the cache in a safe test. Observe source traffic, latency and errors. A warm hit-rate chart alone does not prove the architecture can recover. Here is a challenge. An event title changes but users still see the old title. Explain two remedies. Pause before the answer. Invalidate or version the affected cache entry on a successful update, or accept the documented TTL staleness. Consider races between refill and update; test the chosen consistency behavior. For an interview, choose key scope, invalidation and stampede control. Say what you would measure, not only which tool you would buy.

caching.narration: Kokoro v1.0 · af_heart · pre-generated English female voice

chapters.title: Build an intuition
chapters.text: Let us understand cdn. A publisher places copies of a book in many nearby libraries. A student borrows locally instead of travelling to the printing factory. A personalized sealed letter should not be put on the shared shelf. Similarly, images and versioned scripts differ from private booking responses. A content delivery network serves suitable content from locations closer to users. It can cache public assets and reduce origin traffic. It does not make private or rapidly changing data safe to cache automatically.

chapters.title: Follow the normal path
chapters.text: Follow the normal path. A visitor requests a public poster. The content delivery network routes the request to a suitable edge location rather than always going directly to the origin. If the edge has a valid copy, it returns that representation. This can reduce both response latency and repeated origin transfer. SeatSpot posters and JavaScript bundles are useful near visitors. The booking API still needs authorization, correct seat state and an explicit cache policy.

chapters.title: Predict a failure
chapters.text: Now change one condition. A missing or expired representation needs an origin fetch. The origin and its network path still matter for uncached work. A common misunderstanding is this: A CDN removes the origin from every request. Cache misses and dynamic requests still depend on the origin. Think about this. Can an account response use the same public cache policy as a versioned stylesheet? Pause the video and make your prediction. No. Private representations need deliberate cache keys and policies. Shared caching can leak another user’s response.

chapters.title: Work through an example
chapters.text: Let us reason with a concrete example. An illustrative 1 MB poster is requested 10,000 times. Uncached origin transfer would be about 10 GB in decimal units. A 90% edge hit rate would reduce those origin payload reads to roughly 1 GB, ignoring overhead and refresh behavior. Use explicit public asset policies and versioned filenames; treat booking/account routes separately. Costs, topology and actual hit rate depend on the provider and workload. These figures are teaching examples, not production guarantees.

chapters.title: Choose and apply
chapters.text: Turn the idea into a design decision. When asset bytes change, publish a new content-versioned name. Long-lived immutable caching only fits a URL whose content will not change. An account or booking response may be personal and time-sensitive. Do not place it on the shared public cache path without a deliberately safe policy. When you try the practice task, look for this result. A content-hashed public file is a suitable immutable candidate; the account statement is not.

chapters.title: Explain it back
chapters.text: Check your understanding. Compare edge hits, misses and private requests separately. A fast cached poster does not show whether the booking API meets its latency and correctness objectives. Here is a challenge. A new logo is uploaded at the old immutable URL but users see the previous one. What is a safer release approach? Pause before the answer. Deploy the new asset under a content-versioned URL and update references. Confirm the production deployment, response headers and edge behavior; invalidate legacy copies if necessary. For an interview, defend cache keys, expiry and invalidation. Say what you would measure, not only which tool you would buy.

chapters.title: Build an intuition
chapters.text: Let us understand api gateway. A school reception desk checks visitor identity and sends visitors to the right office. Passing reception does not mean a visitor can open every cupboard. Services still decide which records or actions that person is permitted to access. An API gateway is an entry layer that applies shared API policies and routes requests to services. Authentication, quotas and request validation may live there, but business authorization still belongs near the protected data.

chapters.title: Follow the normal path
chapters.text: Follow the normal path. The client calls a public API address. The gateway provides a shared routing boundary instead of requiring clients to know every internal service location. Validate the request and supported identity credentials with maintained security libraries. Reject oversized or invalid traffic before forwarding expensive work. SeatSpot exposes event, order and payment services through one public API. Shared routing and coarse policies can be managed consistently, while each service owns its business rules.

chapters.title: Predict a failure
chapters.text: Now change one condition. Event requests go to the event service; order requests go to the order service. API versions and paths should have deliberate routing rules. A common misunderstanding is this: The gateway replaces all service authorization. Each service must protect its business actions and resources. Think about this. A valid user changes /orders/17 to /orders/18. Which boundary must still verify ownership? Pause the video and make your prediction. The order service or data-access boundary must authorize that record. Passing gateway authentication is insufficient.

chapters.title: Work through an example
chapters.text: Let us reason with a concrete example. A mobile screen calls events and orders through one gateway. Its latency includes gateway work plus downstream waits. Two parallel calls take approximately the slower path plus overhead; two sequential calls add their delays. Real dependency behavior and timeouts determine the result. Keep routing/coarse policy central but preserve domain authorization and tracing in services. Test a gateway outage and a single unhealthy downstream service. These figures are teaching examples, not production guarantees.

chapters.title: Choose and apply
chapters.text: Turn the idea into a design decision. The order service checks ownership and allowed actions using verified identity. Passing gateway authentication does not grant access to another visitor order. If one API request fans out, set deadlines and partial-failure behavior. A slow optional service should not hold every gateway worker indefinitely. When you try the practice task, look for this result. A verified identity does not grant access to every record.

chapters.title: Explain it back
chapters.text: Check your understanding. Trace requests through the boundary and test gateway capacity and redundancy. Centralizing policy is useful, but it also creates an important operational dependency. Here is a challenge. A signed-in user changes an order ID in the URL. Which component must stop cross-user access? Pause before the answer. The order service must perform resource-level authorization using verified identity. Gateway checks are useful but cannot replace ownership enforcement. For an interview, explain token checks, quotas, deadlines and resource ownership. Say what you would measure, not only which tool you would buy.

api-gateway.narration: Kokoro v1.0 · af_heart · pre-generated English female voice

chapters.title: Build an intuition
chapters.text: Let us understand rate limiting. A library lets each student borrow a limited number of books so one student cannot empty the shelves. A short burst may be acceptable, but repeated borrowing must remain within a fair rate. The rule needs a reliable way to identify the student, not just the colour of their shoes. Rate limiting controls how much work an identity or client may request over time. It protects capacity and fairness, but it is not a complete defense against every attack.

chapters.title: Follow the normal path
chapters.text: Follow the normal path. Requests are assigned a deliberate identity key, such as a verified account and endpoint. A spoofable header cannot safely define a protected client budget. The token bucket refills over elapsed time up to its capacity. Capacity permits a bounded burst while the refill rate controls sustained use. SeatSpot protects sign-in and booking attempts from excessive traffic. Public browsing, expensive searches and paid customers may need different budgets; one shared limit for everyone can punish unrelated users.

chapters.title: Predict a failure
chapters.text: Now change one condition. Checking and consuming a token must behave as one operation for shared state. Separate reads and writes can overspend under concurrency. A common misunderstanding is this: An IP header is always a reliable user identity. Client-controlled forwarding headers can be forged, and many people share one NAT address. Think about this. Ten tokens are spent immediately. After three idle seconds at two tokens/second, how many tokens remain? Pause the video and make your prediction. Six, capped by the bucket capacity of ten. Concurrent updates need an atomic implementation to preserve that rule.

chapters.title: Work through an example
chapters.text: Let us reason with a concrete example. A teaching token bucket has capacity 10 and refills at 2 tokens/second. If initially full, ten immediate requests can consume ten tokens. After 3 idle seconds it has six tokens, capped at ten. This model ignores distributed races until an atomic implementation is chosen. Choose a key and storage behavior explicitly. Protect critical actions with a deliberate fail-closed or degraded policy rather than silently giving unlimited access after a store failure. These figures are teaching examples, not production guarantees.

chapters.title: Choose and apply
chapters.text: Turn the idea into a design decision. A request with enough tokens proceeds, but still faces authorization, request validation and downstream concurrency limits. Passing the limiter is not a correctness guarantee. A request without budget receives a clear rejection and retry guidance where appropriate. Clients should wait rather than creating an immediate retry storm. When you try the practice task, look for this result. Only the available budget is admitted; a 429 response can communicate a retry policy.

chapters.title: Explain it back
chapters.text: Check your understanding. If the shared limiter fails, enforce the chosen endpoint policy and alert. Independent local counters do not preserve a strict global quota across replicas. Here is a challenge. Three replicas each allow 100 requests/minute for one user. Is the global user limit 100? Pause before the answer. Not with independent counters: the user may receive up to roughly 300 across replicas, depending on routing and windows. Use an atomic shared budget or state explicitly that the policy is per instance. For an interview, choose a principal, atomic state and store-failure policy. Say what you would measure, not only which tool you would buy.

rate-limiting.narration: Kokoro v1.0 · af_heart · pre-generated English female voice

chapters.title: Build an intuition
chapters.text: Let us understand circuit breaker. A home fuse interrupts an unsafe circuit instead of letting every appliance keep drawing current. A software breaker is not the same physical mechanism, but the useful idea is similar: stop repeated harmful attempts, observe conditions and restore access carefully. A circuit breaker temporarily stops calls to a dependency that appears unhealthy, then cautiously tests recovery. It prevents repeated waiting and extra pressure; it does not repair the dependency.

chapters.title: Follow the normal path
chapters.text: Follow the normal path. The breaker allows normal calls and records eligible outcomes. Timeouts still bound each attempt; a closed breaker is not a guarantee of health. The dependency times out repeatedly. A minimum sample and measurement window help distinguish a pattern from a single unlucky request. If SeatSpot recommendations repeatedly time out, continuing to call them can occupy every connection. A breaker can reject or use a safe optional fallback while core booking work continues.

chapters.title: Predict a failure
chapters.text: Now change one condition. The breaker opens and rejects dependency calls quickly. This frees local resources and avoids repeating expensive failures while recovery is investigated. A common misunderstanding is this: An open breaker makes every fallback safe. A fallback must preserve business meaning; it cannot fabricate a successful payment. Think about this. The breaker opens. Has it repaired the failed payment provider? Pause the video and make your prediction. No. It stops repeated calls quickly. Recovery probes only test whether the dependency can be used again.

chapters.title: Work through an example
chapters.text: Let us reason with a concrete example. An illustrative breaker opens after enough samples show a 50% eligible-failure rate in its window. A minimum of 20 calls avoids opening after one failure out of one call in this example. The numbers are teaching choices, not recommended universal settings. Define which timeouts/errors count, limit half-open probes and watch false trips alongside recovery time. These figures are teaching examples, not production guarantees.

chapters.title: Choose and apply
chapters.text: Turn the idea into a design decision. Optional recommendations can be omitted. Essential payment outcomes must remain pending or failed according to verified state, not invented to hide the outage. After a reset interval, allow a limited probe set. Sending every waiting caller at once can overload a dependency that is only partly recovered. When you try the practice task, look for this result. Few probes avoid a recovery stampede; thresholds are workload choices.

chapters.title: Explain it back
chapters.text: Check your understanding. Successful probes restore normal traffic; failed probes reopen the breaker. Observe both false trips and recovery behavior under controlled failure tests. Here is a challenge. What should a breaker do after the reset interval? Pause before the answer. Move to half-open with bounded probes. Evaluate actual outcomes before restoring full traffic; otherwise recovering capacity may be overwhelmed again. For an interview, define eligible failures, thresholds and bounded probes. Say what you would measure, not only which tool you would buy.

chapters.title: Build an intuition
chapters.text: Let us understand message queues. A restaurant writes orders on tickets. The cook takes a ticket when ready instead of making every customer stand at the stove. A ticket can be picked up twice after confusion, so the kitchen needs an order number to avoid preparing and charging the same order twice. A message queue holds work until a consumer can process it. It separates accepting work from finishing it. Durability, retries, ordering and duplicate delivery depend on the queue and configuration.

chapters.title: Follow the normal path
chapters.text: Follow the normal path. A booking succeeds and records a receipt job reliably. Coordinate this with business storage, for example using an outbox, so a crash does not lose the obligation. The queue stores work while consumers catch up. Stored backlog buys time, but retention, storage and acceptable delay remain finite. SeatSpot sends receipts asynchronously after booking. The booking request should not wait for an email provider, but it must reliably record that a receipt needs to be sent.

chapters.title: Predict a failure
chapters.text: Now change one condition. Workers pull jobs at a safe rate. Their combined concurrency must respect email provider quotas and other downstream capacity. A common misunderstanding is this: At-least-once delivery means exactly one business effect. Delivery and the external effect have different failure gaps. Think about this. A worker sends a receipt then crashes before acknowledgment. What can happen next? Pause the video and make your prediction. The job may be delivered again. A stable event ID and appropriate idempotency or reconciliation are needed around the external effect.

chapters.title: Work through an example
chapters.text: Let us reason with a concrete example. Jobs arrive at 90/second and each worker safely processes 20/second. Four workers provide 80/second, so backlog grows by about 10/second. Five provide 100/second and drain only about 10/second of existing backlog in the simplified model. Add safe capacity or shed work, respecting the email provider quota. More consumers are not safe if they collectively exceed the next dependency limit. These figures are teaching examples, not production guarantees.

chapters.title: Choose and apply
chapters.text: Turn the idea into a design decision. A worker can send an email and fail before acknowledging its job. The queue may deliver that same logical job again. Use stable job identity and an appropriate idempotency or reconciliation strategy. A delivery guarantee alone does not guarantee exactly one external effect. When you try the practice task, look for this result. At a constant arrival rate, five workers leave only about ten jobs/second to drain the backlog.

chapters.title: Explain it back
chapters.text: Check your understanding. After bounded attempts, move a poison job to a monitored dead-letter path. Investigate and repair before controlled replay instead of retrying forever. Here is a challenge. A worker sends an email then crashes before acknowledging. What happens? Pause before the answer. Redelivery may send another email unless the consumer/provider has an idempotency or deduplication strategy. A durable order/event identity and reconciliation make this case explicit. For an interview, discuss backlog age, retries, poison jobs and idempotency. Say what you would measure, not only which tool you would buy.

chapters.title: Build an intuition
chapters.text: Let us understand event-driven architecture. A school posts that sports day has been confirmed. Teachers arrange transport, the canteen plans food and students bring equipment. The announcement is one fact with several independent reactions. If the date is corrected, people need a clear update rather than silently rewriting an announcement they already acted on. In event-driven architecture, components announce facts that happened and other components react. An event such as BookingConfirmed differs from a command such as ConfirmBooking, which asks an owner to perform an action.

chapters.title: Follow the normal path
chapters.text: Follow the normal path. The booking owner establishes that the booking is confirmed, then reliably publishes the associated fact. Publication and storage must have an explicit failure strategy. The event channel makes the fact available to separate subscribers. Each subscriber has a distinct business responsibility and its own processing state. SeatSpot booking confirmation can trigger receipts, analytics and loyalty updates without the booking service synchronously calling every consumer. This reduces direct coupling but introduces asynchronous coordination.

chapters.title: Predict a failure
chapters.text: Now change one condition. Analytics becomes slow while receipt processing continues. Subscriber delay is observable; it should not silently redefine the original booking outcome. A common misunderstanding is this: Publishing an event creates one atomic transaction across subscribers. Independent consumers have separate state, delay and failure boundaries. Think about this. BookingConfirmed is replayed. Should every subscriber repeat its old external action? Pause the video and make your prediction. No. Rebuilding analytics and resending old receipts have different consequences. Each consumer needs an explicit replay policy.

chapters.title: Work through an example
chapters.text: Let us reason with a concrete example. BookingConfirmed has receipt, analytics and loyalty subscribers. A failed analytics consumer should not roll back a valid booking. Loyalty may remain eventually consistent, while seat ownership must stay authoritative. Document each subscriber obligation and recovery/replay rules. Replaying an analytics event is different from sending every historical receipt again. These figures are teaching examples, not production guarantees.

chapters.title: Choose and apply
chapters.text: Turn the idea into a design decision. A repeated delivery uses the same logical event identity. Consumers must avoid awarding points or producing another external effect accidentally. Add compatible fields carefully and test old consumers. Retained events and delayed subscribers may outlive the latest deployment. When you try the practice task, look for this result. A repeated event must not award loyalty points twice; replay is a business decision.

chapters.title: Explain it back
chapters.text: Check your understanding. Replay analytics when appropriate, but do not resend historical receipts automatically. Reprocessing policy depends on the side effects owned by each subscriber. Here is a challenge. A loyalty consumer receives BookingConfirmed twice. What must remain true? Pause before the answer. The booking should earn the intended points once. Deduplicate or make the update idempotent within a durable transaction; account for partial failure around external effects. For an interview, discuss versioned contracts, lag and idempotent consumers. Say what you would measure, not only which tool you would buy.

chapters.title: Build an intuition
chapters.text: Let us understand database replication. Two students copy notes from one teacher. If copying takes time, one notebook may lack the last sentence. If the teacher accidentally deletes an important page and the students copy that deletion, every notebook can lose it. You still need a recoverable older copy. Replication keeps copies of database data. It can improve resilience or serve reads, but asynchronous copies may lag. A replica is not the same as an independent backup.

chapters.title: Follow the normal path
chapters.text: Follow the normal path. A booking write reaches the current primary. Its acknowledgment policy determines what the application can assume about durability and replication at that moment. Changes travel to replicas. With asynchronous replication, the primary can reply before all copies have applied the latest write. SeatSpot may serve public catalog reads from replicas while routing authoritative reservations to the write owner. A user reading immediately after a write must not be surprised by a stale confirmation state.

chapters.title: Predict a failure
chapters.text: Now change one condition. A confirmation read reaches Replica A before the booking arrives there. The user may see an older state even though the primary accepted the write. A common misunderstanding is this: Replication protects against every accidental deletion. A replica can copy the same deletion or corruption. Keep restore-tested recovery points separately. Think about this. The primary confirms at 12:00:00; the replica applies at 12:00:02. What can a read at 12:00:01 show? Pause the video and make your prediction. The earlier state, even though the primary accepted the write. Read-your-writes requires a suitable authoritative or documented consistency path.

chapters.title: Work through an example
chapters.text: Let us reason with a concrete example. The primary confirms a booking at 12:00:00. A read replica applies it at 12:00:02. A read at 12:00:01 may see the earlier state. Two seconds here is fictional teaching lag, not a product guarantee. Read the confirmation from an authoritative path or implement a documented consistency mechanism. Do not tell the user their purchase disappeared simply because a replica is behind. These figures are teaching examples, not production guarantees.

chapters.title: Choose and apply
chapters.text: Turn the idea into a design decision. Use the primary or an explicitly supported consistency mechanism for confirmation. Public catalog reads can have a different staleness allowance. If the primary fails, promotion needs a clear election or orchestration process and fencing. Avoid letting an isolated old writer accept conflicting new changes. When you try the practice task, look for this result. Lag is different from a failed purchase; a replica is not an independent historical backup.

chapters.title: Explain it back
chapters.text: Check your understanding. Replication also copies many mistakes. Maintain tested backups and recovery points independently rather than counting live copies as protection against every kind of data loss. Here is a challenge. Why can a replica show an order as missing just after checkout? Pause before the answer. Asynchronous replication may not have applied the write yet. Route that confirmation to an appropriate authoritative path or use a supported read-your-writes mechanism. Distinguish lag from a real failed write. For an interview, compare acknowledgment, read consistency and failover fencing. Say what you would measure, not only which tool you would buy.

chapters.title: Build an intuition
chapters.text: Let us understand database sharding. A library splits books across buildings by a catalog rule. The catalog must tell you which building owns a book. A rule that sends every popular book to the same building still creates a queue. Finding books across all buildings is more work than visiting one shelf. Sharding divides records across separate database shards, often using a key. Each record needs a known home. It can spread storage and write load, but cross-shard operations and moving data become harder.

chapters.title: Follow the normal path
chapters.text: Follow the normal path. A request carries a tenant or entity key. The routing rule maps that key to an authoritative shard before data is read or written. Different record groups live on different database shards. This can spread storage and write work when the groups are actually independent enough. SeatSpot may eventually outgrow one database write/storage boundary. Sharding could place different tenants or events on different shards, but one extremely popular event can still create a hot shard.

chapters.title: Predict a failure
chapters.text: Now change one condition. One popular event can overload its shard even when every shard has the same row count. Workload distribution matters more than counting keys. A common misunderstanding is this: Hashing guarantees equal load. It distributes keys; uneven popularity and request cost can still make a hot shard. Think about this. Four shards have similar row counts, but one tenant sends half the traffic. Is the workload balanced? Pause the video and make your prediction. Not necessarily. Even row distribution is different from even traffic. A hot tenant may still dominate one shard.

chapters.title: Work through an example
chapters.text: Let us reason with a concrete example. Ten tenants each produce similar load except one tenant generates half the total. Hashing tenant IDs across four shards can still put half the traffic on the hot tenant shard. Even key counts do not mean even traffic. Consider splitting that tenant workload using a suitable finer key, isolation or an alternative ownership model. Test query patterns and transaction boundaries before committing. These figures are teaching examples, not production guarantees.

chapters.title: Choose and apply
chapters.text: Turn the idea into a design decision. A query across all events may contact every shard and merge results. Cross-shard joins, transactions and uniqueness require deliberate support or redesign. Rebalancing needs copying, verification, a write/cutover policy and an updated routing map. Changing a modulo number does not move existing records. When you try the practice task, look for this result. A routing function alone does not migrate records, rebalance a hot tenant or preserve cross-shard transactions.

chapters.title: Explain it back
chapters.text: Check your understanding. Shard only when requirements and measurements justify the coordination cost. A suitable index or larger database may solve the current problem with much less complexity. Here is a challenge. One event causes 70% of booking writes and eventId is the shard key. Does adding shards fix it? Pause before the answer. Not automatically. That event remains on one shard. Revisit seat ownership/partitioning and concurrency rules, or provide dedicated capacity, without weakening atomic reservation correctness. For an interview, choose a key and discuss joins, transactions and hot tenants. Say what you would measure, not only which tool you would buy.

chapters.title: Build an intuition
chapters.text: Let us understand data partitioning. You organize school papers into folders by month. Finding November work becomes easier if you open only the November folder. Putting every folder on the same desk does not create more desks. Likewise, smaller table parts can improve maintenance or pruning without adding another database machine. Partitioning splits a dataset into manageable parts using rules such as date ranges or key hashes. Table partitions can remain inside one database; partitioning does not automatically mean physical sharding across servers.

chapters.title: Follow the normal path
chapters.text: Follow the normal path. History rows are grouped by date. This organization can exist inside one database and should not be confused with distributing ownership across independent shards. Each month has a defined range with explicit boundaries. Future data needs a matching partition or a deliberately configured default behavior. SeatSpot stores an increasing audit/history table. Date partitions can make retention and time-bounded queries easier while keeping current reservation transactions on an appropriate authoritative path.

chapters.title: Predict a failure
chapters.text: Now change one condition. A date-bounded query reaches the planner. The engine can eliminate irrelevant ranges if its rules and the query expression permit partition pruning. A common misunderstanding is this: Table partitioning automatically scales across machines. Partitions can remain inside the same database on the same machine. Think about this. A monthly partitioned table is queried without a date predicate. Must it read only one month? Pause the video and make your prediction. No. Without a usable condition the database may inspect many partitions. Check the query plan instead of assuming pruning.

chapters.title: Work through an example
chapters.text: Let us reason with a concrete example. History contains one million rows per month over two years. A query requests one month. With useful pruning it may inspect a relevant partition rather than all 24 million rows, but actual I/O depends on predicates, indexes and plans. Use EXPLAIN in a test environment. Confirm pruning and retention behavior instead of assuming a partitioned table is always faster. These figures are teaching examples, not production guarantees.

chapters.title: Choose and apply
chapters.text: Turn the idea into a design decision. The November partition supplies the requested history. An appropriate index and query plan can still be necessary inside that partition. Retention can operate on old partitions, but removal is a data-policy decision. Verify dependencies, recovery requirements and correct boundaries before destructive maintenance. When you try the practice task, look for this result. Partitioning can aid pruning and lifecycle management without adding another database server.

chapters.title: Explain it back
chapters.text: Check your understanding. A query without the partition key may still inspect many parts. More partitions do not automatically add machines, guarantee speed or fix one hot-row lock. Here is a challenge. A table is partitioned by date, but a query filters only customer email. Must it be fast? Pause before the answer. No. The engine may inspect many partitions without a useful date restriction. Examine the actual plan and indexing/access pattern rather than assuming partitioning alone helps. For an interview, discuss partition keys, pruning, indexes and retention. Say what you would measure, not only which tool you would buy.

chapters.title: Build an intuition
chapters.text: Let us understand microservices. A school has a library team, accounts team and transport team. Each owns a different responsibility and communicates through clear requests. If every tiny task needs a meeting with every team, work becomes slower. More teams are helpful only when their boundaries reduce coordination rather than create it. Microservices split a system into independently deployable business services. The useful boundary is ownership of a capability and its data, not an arbitrary number of small functions or servers.

chapters.title: Follow the normal path
chapters.text: Follow the normal path. Name business responsibilities before drawing services. Catalog descriptions and authoritative seat reservations have different ownership and correctness requirements. Each capability owns its protected state and exposes contracts. Giving every service write access to every table defeats much of the intended independence. SeatSpot may separate booking, catalog and notifications when team ownership, scaling or deployment needs justify it. A small team can often start with a modular monolith and preserve those boundaries without network overhead.

chapters.title: Predict a failure
chapters.text: Now change one condition. The booking workflow contacts payments. That call can time out or succeed remotely while its response is lost; it is not a local transaction. A common misunderstanding is this: Every function should become a microservice. Fine-grained network boundaries can add latency, coordination and partial failures without useful autonomy. Think about this. Catalog, booking and payment must deploy together after every change. Are they operationally independent? Pause the video and make your prediction. Probably not yet. Inspect shared schemas and contracts before calling separate processes independent services.

chapters.title: Work through an example
chapters.text: Let us reason with a concrete example. A confirmation requires catalog lookup, seat reservation, payment and notification. Putting all four behind sequential network calls increases latency and failure combinations. Notification can be asynchronous; reservation/payment need an explicit state machine and reconciliation. Start with the required invariant and workflow. Separate a capability only when the autonomy benefit outweighs the distributed coordination cost. These figures are teaching examples, not production guarantees.

chapters.title: Choose and apply
chapters.text: Turn the idea into a design decision. Confirmation can publish notification work after reliable business-state coordination. A slow email provider need not occupy the booking request indefinitely. Old and new callers may coexist. Test contract compatibility and observe version-specific errors instead of requiring every service to deploy in lockstep. When you try the practice task, look for this result. Separate deployment earns its complexity only when ownership and autonomy are useful.

chapters.title: Explain it back
chapters.text: Check your understanding. For a small team, a modular monolith may satisfy the same domain boundaries with fewer moving parts. Choose services from requirements rather than fashion. Here is a challenge. A two-person team has low traffic and no independent deployment needs. Must it use microservices? Pause before the answer. No. A modular monolith can keep clear domains with simpler transactions and operations. Revisit extraction when measured scaling, ownership or release constraints justify it. For an interview, discuss contracts, state machines and asynchronous notification. Say what you would measure, not only which tool you would buy.

chapters.title: Build an intuition
chapters.text: Let us understand service discovery. A school directory lists which rooms currently host each club. Students ask for the chess club rather than memorizing an old room number. The directory can become stale, so someone must update it and decide what happens when a listed room is closed. Service discovery maps a stable service name to current usable destinations. Instances change as they deploy, fail or scale. Discovery finds candidates; routing and health policies decide how requests reach them.

chapters.title: Follow the normal path
chapters.text: Follow the normal path. The caller requests the payment capability by service name instead of storing an individual pod address that may disappear during the next deployment. The platform or registry tracks service destinations and readiness. Registration and removal need reliable ownership and observable convergence. SeatSpot booking replicas should find the payment service even when its pod addresses change. Hard-coded ephemeral IPs become stale during routine operations.

chapters.title: Predict a failure
chapters.text: Now change one condition. Client or server routing selects a usable endpoint. Discovery and load balancing cooperate, but they describe different responsibilities. A common misunderstanding is this: Finding an endpoint authorizes access to it. Discovery provides destinations, not identity or business permissions. Think about this. DNS resolves the payment service. Does that prove every connection will succeed? Pause the video and make your prediction. No. Name resolution can succeed while endpoints are unhealthy, changing or unreachable. Timeouts and failure handling still apply.

chapters.title: Work through an example
chapters.text: Let us reason with a concrete example. Three payment pods are replaced during a rolling deployment. Their individual IPs may change while a Kubernetes Service name remains stable. Endpoint/readiness propagation and existing connections still create a transition interval. Use the platform service abstraction and test replacement with live requests. Do not promise instantaneous convergence from a stable name. These figures are teaching examples, not production guarantees.

chapters.title: Choose and apply
chapters.text: Turn the idea into a design decision. An old instance becomes unready and a replacement joins. Cached addresses and existing connections can outlive the registry update. A failed connection may use a safe bounded retry against current membership. Do not hide repeated errors with unlimited retries. When you try the practice task, look for this result. Stable naming helps callers, but does not imply instantaneous endpoint convergence.

chapters.title: Explain it back
chapters.text: Check your understanding. Knowing an address does not authorize a request. Validate the relevant identity, transport security and resource permissions at the appropriate boundaries. Here is a challenge. DNS resolves the service but requests fail. What do you check next? Pause before the answer. Check ready endpoints, target port, network reachability/policy, TLS identity and the dependency itself. Compare resolution with an actual bounded request and inspect traces. For an interview, compare client-side selection with a stable service/proxy address. Say what you would measure, not only which tool you would buy.

chapters.title: Build an intuition
chapters.text: Let us understand reverse proxy. A reception desk receives mail for several offices and forwards each envelope internally. Outside visitors know the public address rather than every room. The desk must preserve important information and must not believe a forged note saying that an envelope came from the principal. A reverse proxy receives requests on behalf of backend servers and forwards them. It can terminate TLS, route paths or hosts and manage forwarding behavior. It is different from a forward proxy used on behalf of clients.

chapters.title: Follow the normal path
chapters.text: Follow the normal path. The browser talks to one public address. The reverse proxy represents backend servers rather than acting as the browser own outbound proxy. Host and path rules select a backend. Request size, deadlines, TLS termination and supported protocols must fit the actual workload. SeatSpot can expose one HTTPS hostname while forwarding application and static paths to different backends. This central entry layer needs deliberate timeout, buffering and trusted-header behavior.

chapters.title: Predict a failure
chapters.text: Now change one condition. API traffic reaches the API backend and asset traffic can reach another backend. A reverse proxy can also perform load-balancing duties. A common misunderstanding is this: A reverse proxy and load balancer cannot be the same component. These are roles that can overlap in one product. Think about this. A client sends X-Forwarded-For claiming to be an administrator. Should your backend trust it? Pause the video and make your prediction. Only through a verified proxy chain with controlled header rewriting. A client-supplied header is not trusted identity.

chapters.title: Work through an example
chapters.text: Let us reason with a concrete example. A browser uploads a large image through a proxy to the application. The application body limit does not help if the proxy rejects it first; conversely, a permissive proxy does not bypass the application validation. The smallest relevant limit wins. Align intended limits and return understandable errors. For streaming, inspect buffering and timeouts along the full path. These figures are teaching examples, not production guarantees.

chapters.title: Choose and apply
chapters.text: Turn the idea into a design decision. Forward useful request context, but do not accept forged identity or client-IP headers from arbitrary clients as trusted facts. Buffering and idle/read timeouts can change what a browser sees. Test streams and long-lived connections end to end instead of assuming default behavior fits. When you try the practice task, look for this result. The narrowest relevant limit can reject the request; streaming needs deliberate buffering and timeout choices.

chapters.title: Explain it back
chapters.text: Check your understanding. The public entry point needs its own capacity, redundancy and monitoring. Backend replicas do not help if the only proxy is unavailable. Here is a challenge. An API stream produces tokens but the browser sees them all at once. What might be happening? Pause before the answer. A proxy/CDN may buffer the response. Verify streaming support, flush behavior, timeout and cache/compression policies across the actual path before changing application logic blindly. For an interview, discuss TLS termination, headers, limits and connection draining. Say what you would measure, not only which tool you would buy.

chapters.title: Build an intuition
chapters.text: Let us understand dns management. A phone book maps a name to a number. People who wrote down yesterday number may keep using it until they check again. Changing the book cannot hang up every current call. DNS caches and existing network connections behave similarly. DNS translates names into records such as addresses. Managing DNS includes authoritative records, TTL, delegation and safe changes. It is not an HTTP redirect and does not instantly move every existing connection.

chapters.title: Follow the normal path
chapters.text: Follow the normal path. The browser or operating system asks a resolver for the hostname. Existing local or resolver caches may already contain an answer. A resolver without a usable cached answer follows DNS resolution to the authoritative records. Record type and delegation must be configured correctly. SeatSpot changes an application endpoint or validates a domain. A safe release must account for record type, current TTL, certificate/host configuration and rollback rather than assuming Save means every user changed immediately.

chapters.title: Predict a failure
chapters.text: Now change one condition. A client may connect to the old endpoint while its answer is still valid. Changing the authoritative record does not instantly erase that cached answer. A common misunderstanding is this: DNS is an HTTP redirect. DNS provides records before the HTTP connection; a redirect is a later HTTP response. Think about this. A resolver cached a one-hour answer ten minutes ago. Does lowering TTL now erase its cache? Pause the video and make your prediction. No. That cached answer can remain until its old expiry. The shorter TTL applies to answers fetched later.

chapters.title: Work through an example
chapters.text: Let us reason with a concrete example. A record was cached at 10:00 with a 3,600 second TTL. You lower TTL at 10:10. That existing cache may retain the old answer until about 11:00. The new shorter TTL affects later fetched answers, not already cached copies. Reduce TTL in advance when appropriate, prepare both endpoints and monitor the transition. Keep domain ownership, DNS and hosting configuration separate in your explanation. These figures are teaching examples, not production guarantees.

chapters.title: Choose and apply
chapters.text: Turn the idea into a design decision. Later lookups can obtain the new destination. Clients and resolvers change at different times, so old and new endpoints may both receive traffic. The new address also needs the correct certificate, host routing and healthy application. Successful resolution alone does not prove the website works. When you try the practice task, look for this result. The old cached answer can remain until about 11:00; existing connections are a separate issue.

chapters.title: Explain it back
chapters.text: Check your understanding. Keep a rollback path and an appropriate overlap interval. Lower TTL in advance when useful; do not expect a last-second TTL edit to end existing connections. Here is a challenge. Why do two users reach different servers after a DNS update? Pause before the answer. Resolvers fetched answers at different times and may retain previous TTLs. Clients may also reuse existing connections. Inspect records and actual request routing before concluding the update failed. For an interview, discuss A/AAAA/CNAME/TXT, delegation and TTL planning. Say what you would measure, not only which tool you would buy.

chapters.title: Build an intuition
chapters.text: Let us understand disaster recovery. A student keeps a second copy of schoolwork in another safe place and practises opening it on a different computer. Knowing a copy exists is not enough if it is unreadable, its password is lost or it takes days to find. Recovery is the complete ability to resume useful work. Disaster recovery is a tested plan for restoring required service and data after a serious disruption. Define the acceptable recovery time and acceptable data-loss window, then prove your procedure can meet them.

chapters.title: Follow the normal path
chapters.text: Follow the normal path. Define how long the required user operation may be unavailable and how much recent data loss is acceptable. These are explicit business objectives, not product defaults. Capture suitable backups and change logs with recoverable keys and configuration. Live replication alone may copy deletion or corruption to every current replica. SeatSpot needs a response to regional loss, accidental deletion or corruption. Application replicas alone do not restore deleted orders or missing secrets/configuration.

chapters.title: Predict a failure
chapters.text: Now change one condition. A serious failure interrupts the production environment. Recovery needs an environment, permissions and an executable runbook, not merely a promise that a backup exists. A common misunderstanding is this: Replication replaces recovery backups. Replication may reproduce corruption or deletion. Independent recovery points solve a different problem. Think about this. Hourly-only backups are available. Do they satisfy a 15-minute recovery-point objective by themselves? Pause the video and make your prediction. No. The missing-data window can approach an hour. Use a suitable capture/recovery strategy and prove it in a drill.

chapters.title: Work through an example
chapters.text: Let us reason with a concrete example. The business requires an illustrative RTO of 60 minutes and RPO of 15 minutes. Backups run every hour. Hourly-only backups can leave nearly an hour of missing data, exceeding a 15-minute RPO. A 60-minute RTO also includes provisioning, restore, validation and traffic recovery, not just file download time. Select a suitable backup/log capture strategy and rehearse the whole path. Targets are objectives; measured drill results establish whether the current plan meets them. These figures are teaching examples, not production guarantees.

chapters.title: Choose and apply
chapters.text: Turn the idea into a design decision. Rebuild required infrastructure and restore data in a safe environment. Include secrets, certificates, queues and other dependencies required for actual user workflows. Query restored data and run correctness checks. A process reporting restore complete does not prove that bookings, ownership and payment reconciliation are usable. When you try the practice task, look for this result. An existing backup is not proof of a usable recovery plan; measured restoration is the evidence.

chapters.title: Explain it back
chapters.text: Check your understanding. Restore traffic safely and compare measured end-to-end recovery and data loss with the objectives. Record gaps, improve the runbook and repeat the drill. Here is a challenge. A restore finishes in 40 minutes but application validation and routing take another 35. Does it meet a 60-minute RTO? Pause before the answer. No: the measured end-to-end recovery is 75 minutes. Improve or revise the plan based on business requirements and repeat the drill. For an interview, choose a recovery strategy and measure the complete drill. Say what you would measure, not only which tool you would buy.

chapters.title: Build an intuition
chapters.text: Let us understand zero-downtime deployments. A school repairs one classroom while students use another ready room. Moving students before the new room has desks causes disruption. Throwing away the old room key before every class moves makes rollback difficult. Old and new arrangements must coexist safely during the transition. A zero-downtime deployment aims to release a change without interrupting required user operations. Rolling or blue-green rollout helps, but database compatibility, readiness and connection draining are part of the design.

chapters.title: Follow the normal path
chapters.text: Follow the normal path. Visitors use the existing version while the next release is prepared. Establish user-visible metrics and rollback conditions before shifting traffic. Create new capacity without immediately removing all old instances. Download, initialization and dependency setup take time and need spare resources. SeatSpot must release a booking API while active users and old mobile clients remain. New code and old code may run simultaneously against the same data.

chapters.title: Predict a failure
chapters.text: Now change one condition. The readiness gate verifies the instance can serve the intended request. A running process with missing dependencies should not receive normal traffic yet. A common misunderstanding is this: maxUnavailable: 0 guarantees the whole application is correct. It expresses a rollout constraint; readiness, data compatibility and spare capacity remain necessary. Think about this. Old code still reads a column while new code deploys. Can you drop that column immediately? Pause the video and make your prediction. No. Keep old/new versions compatible during coexistence and rollback. Remove obsolete structures only after the transition is proven safe.

chapters.title: Work through an example
chapters.text: Let us reason with a concrete example. Four replicas must remain available; one replacement is created before one old replica is removed. The rollout temporarily needs capacity for five. If no spare capacity exists, readiness and rollout policy can stall. This simple count excludes node limits and dependency capacity. Test old/new coexistence and rollback with real requests. Treat zero downtime as a measured release goal, not an unconditional Kubernetes flag. These figures are teaching examples, not production guarantees.

chapters.title: Choose and apply
chapters.text: Turn the idea into a design decision. Send a bounded share to the new version and drain old work deliberately. Monitor errors and latency for real user operations, not only process health. Both versions can access the database during rollout. Expand and migrate safely before removing fields or behavior the old version still needs. When you try the practice task, look for this result. Rolling back code does not automatically reverse a destructive data migration.

chapters.title: Explain it back
chapters.text: Check your understanding. Stop or reverse traffic movement if the release violates its criteria. Code rollback cannot magically reverse incompatible or destructive data changes. Here is a challenge. Version B renames a database field and Version A still runs. What safer migration sequence can you use? Pause before the answer. Expand with the new field, implement compatible reads/writes, backfill and validate, switch traffic/readers, then contract only when old users are gone. Plan failure/rollback at each step. For an interview, discuss surge capacity, draining and compatible schemas. Say what you would measure, not only which tool you would buy.
