chapters.title: Build an intuition
chapters.text: Let us understand distributed tracing. A parcel carries a tracking number through several delivery centres. Each centre records when its part began and ended. You can find where this parcel waited. That does not mean every parcel took the same path, and missing a tracking scan does not prove the parcel disappeared. Distributed tracing follows one operation across multiple components using linked spans and propagated context. It helps locate time and errors, but traces are sampled evidence, not proof that every request behaved the same way.

chapters.title: Follow the normal path
chapters.text: Follow the normal path. The gateway starts or receives trace context for checkout. Its span represents one part of the operation, not all system traffic. Booking receives compatible context and creates a related span. Without propagation, downstream records can appear as unrelated operations. SeatSpot checkout passes through gateway, booking, database and payment. One total latency number cannot show which hop waited or whether two operations ran in parallel.

chapters.title: Predict a failure
chapters.text: Now change one condition. Database and payment calls run in parallel in this teaching example. Their intervals overlap, so adding both durations would overstate wall-clock time. A common misunderstanding is this: A sampled trace proves every request behaved the same way. Sampling selects evidence, not every operation. Missing context also creates incomplete traces. Think about this. A 100 ms database call overlaps a 300 ms payment call, with 40 ms overhead. Is total duration necessarily 440 ms? Pause the video and make your prediction. No. In the simplified parallel example it is about 340 ms. Inspect overlap and missing time rather than summing every child span.

chapters.title: Work through an example
chapters.text: Let us reason with a concrete example. Checkout has a 100 ms database call and a 300 ms provider call in parallel, plus about 40 ms sequential overhead. A simplified total is about 340 ms, not 440 ms. Actual scheduling, serialization and network effects require measured traces. Investigate the critical path and compare slow traces with broader metrics. Do not optimize a fast database span just because it is easiest to see. These figures are teaching examples, not production guarantees.

chapters.title: Choose and apply
chapters.text: Turn the idea into a design decision. Instrumentation exports spans to an observability backend. Export buffering, sampling and failures mean a trace view is not a complete audit of every request. Compare the critical path, errors and dependency waits. Combine traces with aggregate metrics to determine whether the visible slow request reflects a widespread problem. When you try the practice task, look for this result. Parallel work overlaps in wall-clock time; sampled traces must be compared with aggregate metrics.

chapters.title: Explain it back
chapters.text: Check your understanding. Do not attach secrets or unnecessary personal data to spans. Keep attribute cardinality, access, sampling and retention within a deliberate observability budget. Here is a challenge. Two 200 ms spans run in parallel inside a 250 ms request. Is the request necessarily missing 150 ms? Pause before the answer. No. Parallel spans overlap, so their sum can exceed wall-clock request duration. Inspect start/end times and the critical path before inferring missing time. For an interview, discuss context propagation, critical paths and useful attributes. Say what you would measure, not only which tool you would buy.

chapters.title: Build an intuition
chapters.text: Let us understand network segmentation. A school separates the public reception, classrooms and locked records room. A visitor can enter reception without getting a path to every room. A classroom door being reachable still does not authorize reading a student file. Network access and application permission remain different checks. Network segmentation limits which systems may communicate across network boundaries. It reduces reachability and blast radius. It does not replace identity checks, encryption or resource-level authorization.

chapters.title: Follow the normal path
chapters.text: Follow the normal path. The public client needs the web tier, which needs booking. Booking needs the database. Record required ports and dependencies before introducing isolation. The unrelated worker has no business requirement to contact the orders database. Blocking that path reduces reachability and potential blast radius. SeatSpot public web traffic should not directly reach the orders database or administrative services. Booking may need a narrow database connection while an unrelated image worker does not.

chapters.title: Predict a failure
chapters.text: Now change one condition. Permit the actual booking workload to use the configured database port. Broad namespace-wide rules may allow more callers than intended. A common misunderstanding is this: NetworkPolicy automatically works in every Kubernetes cluster. Enforcement depends on the network implementation and correct selector semantics. Think about this. A database port is reachable from a booking pod. Does that authorize every SQL operation? Pause the video and make your prediction. No. Network reachability is one boundary. Database credentials and application resource authorization still matter.

chapters.title: Work through an example
chapters.text: Let us reason with a concrete example. Only the booking workload should initiate the database application connection on its configured port. A rule allowing the whole namespace may expose more callers than intended; a narrower pod selector can express the required source if labels and enforcement are trustworthy. Test a permitted booking connection and a denied unrelated-worker connection. Also verify DNS and any cross-namespace behavior in the actual cluster. These figures are teaching examples, not production guarantees.

chapters.title: Choose and apply
chapters.text: Turn the idea into a design decision. A policy object is only configuration intent. The cluster network implementation must support and enforce it, and selectors must match the intended workloads. An allowed TCP connection is not permission to read every order. Database credentials, encrypted transport and application ownership checks remain separate controls. When you try the practice task, look for this result. A supporting network implementation must actually enforce the policy; a YAML file alone proves nothing.

chapters.title: Explain it back
chapters.text: Check your understanding. Verify allowed traffic, denied traffic and necessary DNS/monitoring dependencies. Observe unexpected failures and refine the policy without silently opening everything. Here is a challenge. A pod has a NetworkPolicy but unwanted traffic still reaches it. What do you verify? Pause before the answer. Verify enforcement support, labels/selectors, namespace semantics, ingress/egress direction and other allowed rules. Test from the real source workload rather than only inspecting YAML. For an interview, discuss ingress, egress, DNS and actual connection tests. Say what you would measure, not only which tool you would buy.

chapters.title: Build an intuition
chapters.text: Let us understand multi-region setup. A school keeps a working campus in another city. Classes can move after a local disaster, but both campuses must agree which student records are current. If both sell the last seat in the same bus independently, simply having two campuses creates a conflict instead of solving it. A multi-region design runs required components in more than one geographic region. It can support regional recovery or lower user latency, but distant data coordination adds latency, consistency and operational trade-offs.

chapters.title: Follow the normal path
chapters.text: Follow the normal path. Decide whether another region is for disaster recovery, nearby reads or active writes. Each operation can have different latency, availability and consistency requirements. Region A sends changes toward Region B. Asynchronous copying can lag; synchronous coordination adds waiting and depends on the communication path. SeatSpot might serve public catalog reads near users in two regions while keeping seat reservation ownership in one write region. Choosing active-active writes requires an explicit conflict/coordination strategy, not merely deploying the same containers twice.

chapters.title: Predict a failure
chapters.text: Now change one condition. The regions cannot communicate. Allowing both to confirm the same last seat independently can violate correctness even though both applications are running. A common misunderstanding is this: Two regions automatically double availability with no trade-off. Distant coordination adds latency and failure choices; shared dependencies can still fail both. Think about this. Two disconnected regions each see the same last seat. Can both confirm it independently while preserving uniqueness? Pause the video and make your prediction. No. Use a clear owner or coordinated decision, or choose a product model that explicitly accepts and reconciles conflicts.

chapters.title: Work through an example
chapters.text: Let us reason with a concrete example. Two regions can both see one remaining seat while cross-region communication is interrupted. If both independently confirm the seat, availability was preserved but the uniqueness invariant was broken. Preventing that requires a single owner, coordinated decision or a product model that explicitly tolerates/reconciles conflict. Keep authoritative seat allocation under a clear ownership/consistency rule. Use regional catalog caches separately and test failover and failback with realistic lag. These figures are teaching examples, not production guarantees.

chapters.title: Choose and apply
chapters.text: Turn the idea into a design decision. A safe failover establishes which writer owns new decisions and prevents the old writer from conflicting. Routing alone does not settle database ownership. Direct eligible traffic to the recovery region and validate the actual booking workflow. Its capacity, credentials and dependencies must work independently enough for the failure scenario. When you try the practice task, look for this result. A second region is useful only if required dependencies and recovery procedures survive the chosen regional failure.

chapters.title: Explain it back
chapters.text: Check your understanding. After recovery, reconcile lag and in-flight work before moving ownership back. Test both failover and failback instead of treating the first traffic switch as the whole plan. Here is a challenge. Both regions can independently book the last seat during a partition. What requirement is missing? Pause before the answer. There is no safe authoritative allocation/coordination rule for the uniqueness requirement. Define ownership, fencing and the partition policy; refuse or defer some writes if necessary rather than double-sell. For an interview, compare per-operation consistency, routing and recovery objectives. Say what you would measure, not only which tool you would buy.
